summary:
Fire-Orbit is a web platform that uses machine learning to harmonize historical MODIS fire data with current VIIRS data. The model translates MODIS records into VIIRS terms, so both sensors speak the same language and the whole record stays comparable even after MODIS is retired.

We focused on Chile and validated NASA’s detections against CONAF records to confirm they were real fires. Users can explore fire history by year or month and download the data they need. The platform is built for scientists and data analysts at fire prevention organizations like CONAF, for example to decide where to place surveillance cameras in recurring fire hotspots.
details:
• What does it do and how does it work?
    Fire-Orbit is a web platform that uses a machine learning model to harmonize historical MODIS fire data with VIIRS data. The model learns how each sensor detects fires, finds the patterns they share and translates MODIS records into the VIIRS format. Both sensors end up reporting in the same format, so the historical record stays usable even after MODIS is retired.

What benefits does it have?
Scientists and data analysts at fire prevention organizations like CONAF need historical data to identify recurring fire hotspots. Fire-Orbit lets them explore fire history by year or month and download custom reports filtered to exactly what they need. These reports are written in plain language, easy for scientists, data analysts and emergency brigades to read and act on, and help them decide where to install monitoring cameras.

What is the intended impact of the project?
Our focus has two goals:

  1. Harmonize the historical record. MODIS has fire data going back to 2000, while VIIRS only starts in 2012. Translating MODIS into VIIRS terms lets the full history be read as one consistent record.
  2. Reduce the error relative to real fires. VIIRS has higher resolution (375 m vs. about 1 km for MODIS), so its detections are closer to what actually happened on the ground. Bringing MODIS to the VIIRS standard reduces the gap between satellite detections and confirmed fires.

What tools did we use?
Python for data processing and the machine learning model, a hybrid of Random Forest and a recurrent neural network (RNN), which gave the best results both for harmonizing the sensors and when compared against confirmed fires. The web interface uses the standard HTML, CSS and JavaScript stack.

How is our project creative?

  • Validation with ground data: NASA’s satellite detections are cross-checked against records from CONAF, Chile’s national forestry and fire agency, to confirm that each detection was an actual fire and to measure how much the harmonization reduces the error.
  • Sensor translation: Instead of treating MODIS and VIIRS as separate datasets, our model translates one into the other, turning two incompatible records into a single continuous one.
  • Readable reports: Satellite data is turned into plain-language reports that non-specialists can use in the field.

What factors did our team consider?
Fire Radiative Power (FRP), brightness and confidence levels, and how each sensor uses them to decide what counts as a fire. We also considered the difference in resolution between the two sensors and the need to confirm detections against real fire records.
